chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Sinan, from Ismail ibn Jabir who said:

I was in the presence of Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) in Makkah when a messenger from Medina came to him. He said to him, 'Who did you travel with?' He said, 'I did not travel with anyone.' Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'If I had preceded you (or visited you first), I would have taught you good manners.' Then he said, 'One is a Satan, two are two Satans, three are a company, and four are companions.'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the number of companions in Shia hadith regarding social etiquette?
ai.summary: Recorded in *Al-Kafi* from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) in Mecca, this hadith establishes a nuanced taxonomy of social grouping, distinguishing between the vulnerability of the solitary individual and the stability of established companionship. It reflects the Shia emphasis on *Suhbah* (companionship) as a spiritual and social necessity, where the transition from 'two' to 'three' marks the formation of a cohesive unit less prone to discord, thereby guiding believers in maintaining proper etiquette (*Adab*) within their communities.
